column4: When divine guidance comes, whoever follows it will neither go astray nor grieve; the dependent traveller’s safety is made conditional on following guidance.
Believers are shaken by adversity until they ask when God’s help will come; the answer that it is near gives requested aid a crisis scene.
Standing devoutly before God in prayer makes the source’s q-w-m bodily uprightness part of worship itself.
An indirect but concrete reversal of the stalled mount: a passerby is shown his dead donkey restored, so a stopped journey becomes a sign of renewed life.
Jesus names worship of the one Lord as the straight path, repeating the source section’s movement from naʿbudu to the requested road.
Jesus asks who will be his helpers toward God, and the disciples answer that they are God’s helpers; aid becomes companions who stand with a messenger.
Holding fast to God is followed by being guided to a straight path, joining a secure grip to directed movement.
God promises to reinforce the vulnerable believers with sent-down angels, another answer in which help takes the form of supporting companions.
The angelic reinforcement is made good news so hearts may be reassured; its own contribution is the inner steadiness that aid is meant to give.
Threatened believers answer that God is sufficient and the best disposer of affairs, an enacted refusal to seek a less reliable support.
The oppressed weak people cannot devise a plan or find a way, directly naming those who need both help and guidance.
Travel permits a shortened prayer under threat, showing worship itself eased for a vulnerable traveller rather than imposed as an added weight.
By the Book, God leads seekers of His approval along paths of peace, out of darkness and onto a straight path.
Guidance opens the breast, while misguidance constricts it; the source’s supported body has an inner counterpart in expanded or compressed capacity.
The speaker is guided to a straight path described as an upright religion, tightly joining h-d-y to the source’s q-w-m uprightness.
Following the cry for aid in 8:9, this ayah says the angelic response reassures hearts while victory remains from God; it distinguishes the help’s means from its source.
Those who give shelter and help to emigrants become allies of those displaced believers, a social realization of the traveller being held up by others.
The later restatement that migrants and those who shelter and help them are true believers preserves mutual support as a defining communal act.
In the hour of hardship some hearts nearly swerved, yet God turns mercifully toward the Prophet, emigrants, and helpers, preventing inner collapse.
God, who guides to truth, is contrasted with one unable to guide unless first guided; it tests which leader a dependent traveller should follow.
After 11:112’s command to stand firm, this ayah forbids inclining toward wrongdoers and warns that no protector or help remains there.
Jacob again answers loss with “beautiful patience,” extending 12:18’s supported endurance into a second, renewed deprivation.
The messengers admit their human likeness and say believers should rely on God, grounding prophetic action in received favor rather than personal sufficiency.
Satan admits that he merely called and cannot rescue those who followed him; it is a false guide and false helper exposed at the end.
Mountains keep earth from swaying with people, while rivers and paths are made so they may be guided; stable footing and wayfinding are paired.
The Spirit brings revelation to strengthen believers, explicitly naming it both guidance and good news; the guide fortifies the one who receives it.
After forgetting, the Prophet asks that his Lord guide him to what is nearer to right conduct, a precise request for corrected direction.
The ruined garden owner has no group to help him against God and cannot defend himself, exposing support that disappears when it is most needed.
Zachariah says his bones have weakened and turns to God in prayer, a concrete bodily weakness that seeks help without self-reliance.
Firm mountains prevent the earth from swaying with people, and wide paths are set in it so they may be guided: support against wobbling becomes guidance.
The House is purified for those circling, standing, bowing, and prostrating; beside 22:27’s arriving pilgrims, it supplies the upright worship at journey’s end.
The Qur’an is sent in stages to strengthen the Prophet’s heart; the source’s dictionary image of the heart as the body’s support gains a direct Qur’anic counterpart.
God binds Moses’s mother’s heart when grief nearly makes her reveal him, a vivid scene of an inner support preventing a person from giving way.
The Prophet is told to rely on God, who is sufficient as disposer of affairs; reliance is stated as an adequate support for action.
The command to lead the guilty to the path of Hell reverses the life-giving horizon of guidance and warns that being led is not itself salvific.
The Prophet is said to guide to a straight path, identifying the prophetic voice through which a seeker of ihdinā receives direction.
Those who turn back on their heels after guidance has become clear show the reverse movement of the source’s assisted traveller continuing forward.
God sends tranquillity into believers’ hearts so their faith may increase, giving communal firmness an inward support.
The settled believers welcome and prefer the emigrants despite their own need, showing support that lets displaced people continue rather than remain stranded.
“Be helpers of God” is illustrated by Jesus’s disciples answering his call for helpers, a second explicit model of companions lending strength.
The command for “beautiful patience” repeats Jacob’s phrase in 12:18, making patient composure a continuing discipline under pressure.
No one can protect the speaker from God and no refuge exists apart from Him, drawing the boundary around every lesser support.
God knows that the Prophet and believers cannot sustain the full measure of night standing, so He relieves them and commands what is easy of recitation.
God promises to ease the messenger toward ease, a concise divine answer to the source’s passage from strain to supported movement.
God finds the Prophet wandering and guides him, making a person once without a way the recipient of direct divine direction.
Humanity is created in the best taqwīm; this q-w-m form gives the source’s upright body a created, bodily ground.
Being returned to the lowest of the low reverses the upright taqwīm of 95:4, marking how bodily or moral standing can be lost.
